title: Context Language Models: Self-Managing Context to Improve Performance and Reduce Compute Costs
key_facts: Researchers from Meta, MIT and the University of Washington introduce Context Language Models (CLMs), which manage and edit their own context, treating it as a file they can update without restrictions.

It is an alternative to compaction, offloading and retrieval, each of which has limits: summarization can discard critical details, compaction uses predefined rules, and external memory needs the agent to decide what to bring back.

A CLM can rewrite old messages, preserve important facts, remove irrelevant information, keep progress notes and learn its own context-management strategies; users can steer it by telling it the desired strategy.
Three approaches were tested: zero-shot (no specific training), in-context learning with an iterative skill-optimization loop, and reinforcement learning.

Zero-shot CLMs scored 11.4% higher accuracy with 21.5% fewer FLOPs on BrowseComp-Plus, 5% higher with 59% fewer FLOPs on 12-hour EdgeBench, and 65% greater improvement at the same compute on a 24-hour multi-repository agent-swarm task.

In-context learning improved accuracy on ContextBench tasks by up to 35.9 percentage points at lower compute; reinforcement learning lifted Qwen3.5-9B on BrowseComp-Plus from 28.8% to 42.5%, a 47.6% relative improvement, with 12% fewer FLOPs.

The authors acknowledge a CLM may discard information it cannot retrieve, that editable context is a new channel for persistent prompt injections or self-generated instructions, and that more control does not necessarily mean better behavior.
Commenters on X say the results come from specified tasks; a Reddit commenter says CLMs are not production-ready because rewriting context invalidates the model cache.
quote_evidence: Researchers from Meta, MIT, and the University of Washington introduce Context Language Models (CLMs), a new approach that enables language models to manage and edit their own context rather than relying on predefined mechanisms for summarization, compression, and information retrieval, reporting substantial gains in both performance and computational efficiency.
Finally, reinforcement learning improved Qwen3.5-9B performance on BrowseComp-Plus from 28.8% to 42.5%, a 47.6% relative improvement, while using 12% fewer FLOPs.
Most importantly, greater control over context does not necessarily translate into better behavior, as models may still make poor decisions about what to retain, modify, or discard.
why_it_matters_hint: If it holds up, AI agents on long tasks could keep their own notes and drop clutter, cutting computing cost, but the results are the authors' and carry new risks.
event_date: Not stated; InfoQ article listed 11 Oct 2026.
notes: Read InfoQ in full. Research results are the authors' own benchmarks, not independently reproduced; FLOPs (floating-point operations) are a measure of computing work.
